questions.question: In GF(2^8), what operation is used for addition (and subtraction) of two symbols?
options: Bitwise XOR
Integer addition mod 256
Bitwise AND
Rotate-left by 1 bit
questions.explanation: In characteristic-2 fields, addition and subtraction are the same operation: XOR of coefficients.

questions.question: If you add nsym = 10 parity symbols to a message, what is the maximum number of unknown symbol errors you can correct?
questions.explanation: With nsym parity symbols, a Reed-Solomon decoder can correct at most t = floor(nsym/2) unknown symbol errors.

questions.question: What does it mean if all computed syndromes are zero?
options: The received codeword satisfies the parity constraints (no detectable errors)
The message must be all zeros
The generator polynomial is irreducible
The decoder can correct any number of errors
questions.explanation: Syndromes are evaluations at the roots of the generator polynomial; all-zero syndromes mean the received word is a valid codeword for that RS code.

questions.question: Which choice must match between the encoder and the syndrome computation for decoding to work?
options: The generator polynomial roots (evaluation points) used by the code
Only the message length
Only the parity length (nsym)
Only the byte endianness of the machine
questions.explanation: If the encoder and syndrome calculator disagree on field/roots, syndromes won’t correspond to the intended parity constraints.

questions.question: In the decoding pipeline, what does Berlekamp–Massey compute from the syndromes?
options: The error locator polynomial (whose roots identify error positions)
The parity bytes to append during encoding
The corrected message directly
The generator polynomial
questions.explanation: BM synthesizes the minimal-degree locator polynomial consistent with the syndrome sequence.

questions.question: What is Chien search used for in Reed-Solomon decoding?
options: Finding the error positions by locating roots of the locator polynomial
Computing syndromes from a codeword
Computing error magnitudes once positions are known
Generating the GF(256) log/exp tables
questions.explanation: Chien search evaluates the locator polynomial across field powers to find where it becomes zero, which maps to error positions.

questions.question: Why must a practical decoder recompute syndromes after applying corrections?
options: Because beyond the correction radius a decoder can miscorrect, so you must detect failure
Because XOR is not associative
Because RS encoding always changes the message bytes
Because it makes Forney’s algorithm faster
questions.explanation: If the final syndromes are not all zero, the correction was not valid (typically too many errors). Failing closed prevents silent corruption.

questions.question: In this lesson’s implementation, what happens when there are too many symbol errors to correct?
options: Decoding fails with an exception (it does not return a “best effort” message)
The decoder always returns a corrected message anyway
The decoder replaces the whole message with zeros
The decoder switches to integer arithmetic and retries
questions.explanation: The implementation raises on failure (e.g., wrong number of roots or non-zero syndromes after correction), which is the safe behavior.
